references/qpbt-paper/03_proof_overview.tex-67-	After question reduction, the players still respond with $\poly(N)$-length answers, which the verifier has to check satisfies the decision predicate of the original game $\game_z$. The goal of Part (2) is to enable the decision procedure to implement the verification procedure while not requiring the entire full-length answers from the players. In the answer reduction scheme of~\cite{NW19} this is achieved by having the verifier run a \emph{probabilistically checkable proof} (PCP) with the players so that they succinctly \emph{prove} that first, they have introspected questions $(x,y)$ from the correct distribution, and second, that they are able to generate $\poly(N)$-length answers $(a,b)$ that would satisfy the decision predicate of the original game $\game_z$ when executed on $(x,y)$ and $(a,b)$. Since the questions and answers in the PCP are of length $\poly(n)$, this achieves the desired answer length reduction.
references/qpbt-paper/03_proof_overview.tex-68-	
references/qpbt-paper/03_proof_overview.tex-69-	Iterating this scheme presents a number of immediate difficulties that have to do with the fact that the sampling and decision procedures of the verifier in $\game'_z$ do not have such a nice form as those in $\game_z$. First of all, the compression procedure of~\cite{NW19} can only ``introspect'' a specific question distribution of a nonlocal game from~\cite{natarajan2018two}; we call this distribution a ``low-degree test distribution''.\footnote{The nonlocal game of~\cite{natarajan2018two} is part of a more general family of games called ``low-degree tests'', which have been studied extensively for their applications in complexity theory~\cite{babai1991non}, property testing~\cite{rubinfeld1996robust}, and PCPs~\cite{arora1998probabilistic}. Generally, the question distribution of a low-degree test is a random question pair $(x,y)$ where $y$ is a randomly chosen affine subspace in $\F^m$ and $x$ is a uniformly random point on $y$, where $\F$ is a finite field and $m \geq 2$ is an integer. The specific low-degree test game in~\cite{natarajan2018two} (which is based on the low-degree test of~\cite{raz1997sub}) uses two-dimensional subspaces; thus the question distribution of~\cite{raz1997sub,natarajan2018two} is referred to as the ``plane-point distribution''.} However, the resulting question distribution of the question-reduced verifier, which is used to check the introspection, has a much more complex structure. A similar issue arises with the modifications required to perform answer reduction. In the PCP employed to achieve this the question distribution appears to be much more complex than the low-degree test distribution (this is in large part due to the need for a specially tailored PCP procedure that encodes separately different chunks of the witness, corresponding to answers from different players). As a result it is entirely unclear at first whether the question distribution used by the verifier in $\game'_z$ can be ``introspected'' for a second time. 
references/qpbt-paper/03_proof_overview.tex-70-	
references/qpbt-paper/03_proof_overview.tex-71-	To overcome these difficulties we identify a natural class of question distributions, called \emph{conditionally linear distributions}, that generalize the low-degree test distribution. We show that conditionally linear distributions can be ``introspected'' using conditionally linear distributions only, enabling recursive introspection. (In particular, they are a rich enough class to capture the types of question distributions produced by the compression scheme of~\cite{NW19}.) We define normal form verifiers by restricting their sampling procedure to generate conditionally linear question distributions, and this allows us to obtain the compression procedure on normal form verifiers described in Theorem~\ref{thm:compression-informal}.

(As we will see later, other closure properties of conditionally linear distributions, such as taking direct products, play an important role as well.) Since conditionally linear distributions are central to our construction we describe them next.

references/qpbt-paper/03_proof_overview.tex-77-\paragraph{Conditionally linear distributions.} 
references/qpbt-paper/03_proof_overview.tex:78:Fix a vector space $V$ that is identified with $\F^m$, for a finite field $\F$ and integer $m$. Informally (see Definition~\ref{def:cl-func} for a precise definition), a function $L$ on $V$ is \emph{conditionally linear} (CL for short) if it can be evaluated by a procedure that takes the following form: (i) read a substring $z^{(1)}$ of $z$; (ii) evaluate a linear function $L_1$ on $z^{(1)}$; (iii) repeat steps (i) and (ii) with the remaining coordinates $z\backslash z^{(1)}$, such that the next steps are allowed to depend in an arbitrary way on $L_1(z^{(1)})$ but not directly on $z^{(1)}$ itself. What distinguishes a function of this form from an arbitrary function is that we restrict the number of iterations of (i)---(ii) to a constant number (at most $9$, in our case). (One may also think of CL functions as ``adaptively linear'' functions, where the number of ``levels'' of adaptivity is the number of iterations of (i)---(ii).) A distribution $\mu$ over pairs $(x,y) \in V\times V$ is called {conditionally linear}  if it is the image under a pair of {conditionally linear functions} $L^\alice,L^\bob: V\to V$ of the uniform distribution on $V$, i.e.\ $(x,y)\sim (L^\alice(z),L^\bob(z))$ for uniformly random $z\in V$.

references/qpbt-paper/03_proof_overview.tex-80-An important class of CL distributions are low-degree test distributions, which are distributions over question pairs $(x,y)$ where $y$ is a randomly chosen affine subspace of $\F^m$ and $x$ is a uniformly random point on $y$. We explain this for the case where the random subspace $y$ is one-dimensional (i.e.\ a line). Let $V = V_\xpt \oplus V_{\dir{}}$ where $V_\xpt = V_{\dir{}} = \F^m$. Let $L^\alice$ be the projection onto $V_\xpt$ (i.e. it maps $(x,v) \to (x,0)$ where $x \in V_\xpt$ and $v \in V_{\dir{}}$). Define $L^\bob: V \to V$ as the map $(x,v) \mapsto (L^\lnf_v(x),v)$ where $L^\lnf_v: V_\xpt \to V_\xpt$ is a linear map that, for every $v \in V_{\dir{}}$, projects onto a complementary subspace to the one-dimensional subspace of $V_\xpt$ spanned by $v$ (one can think of this as an ``orthogonal subspace'' to the span of $\{ v \}$). $L^\bob$ is conditionally linear because it can be seen as first reading the substring $v \in V_{\dir{}}$ (which can be interpreted as specifying the \emph{direction} of a line), and then applying a linear map $L^\lnf_v$ to $x \in V_\xpt$ (which can be interpreted as specifying a canonical point on the line $\ell = \{ x + tv : t \in \F \}$). It is not hard to see (and shown formally in Section~\ref{sec:ld-game}) that the distribution of $(L^\alice(z),L^\bob(z))$ for $z$ uniform in $V$, is identical (up to relabeling) to the low-degree test distribution $(x,\ell)$ where $\ell$ is a uniformly random affine line in $\F^m$, and $x$ is a uniformly random point on $\ell$.

   679		\uses{def:admissible-size, def:binary-representation,
   680			def:generalized-pauli, def:EPR}
   681		For all admissible field sizes $q = 2^k$ and integers $L$, there exists an

   690		$(\C^2 \ot \C^2)^{\ot Lk}$). Moreover, for all $W \in \{X, Z\}$ and all
   691		$u \in \F_q^L$,

   695			\sigma^W_{u_{ij}}\Bigr)\, \phi\;.
   696		\end{equation}
   697		Here $(u_{ij})_{i,j}$ is the array of $\F_2$ values with

     4	
     5	/-!
     6	# Polynomial preliminaries
     7	
     8	Packages the paper's low-individual-degree polynomial class together
     9	with Schwartz-Zippel bounds as thin wrappers around Mathlib's existing
    10	multivariate polynomial theorems.
    11	
    12	## References
    13	
    14	* `references/ldt-paper/preliminaries.tex`, Section 3 (Preliminaries)
    15	-/
    16	
    17	open Finset Fintype
    18	
    19	open scoped BigOperators
    20	
    21	namespace MIPStarRE.LDT.Preliminaries
    22	
    23	open MvPolynomial
    24	
    25	/-- `\polyfunc{m}{q}{d}` from the paper's definition of low-individual-degree
    26	polynomials. This is Mathlib's `MvPolynomial.restrictDegree` submodule. -/
    27	noncomputable abbrev polyFunc (m : ℕ) (K : Type*) [CommSemiring K] (d : ℕ) :
    28	    Submodule K (MvPolynomial (Fin m) K) :=
    29	  MvPolynomial.restrictDegree (Fin m) K d
    30	
    31	/-- If `p ∈ polyFunc m K d`, then `p.degreeOf i ≤ d` for every variable `i`. -/
    32	theorem degreeOf_le_of_mem_polyFunc {m d : ℕ} {K : Type*} [CommSemiring K]
    33	    {p : MvPolynomial (Fin m) K} (hp : p ∈ polyFunc m K d) (i : Fin m) :
    34	    p.degreeOf i ≤ d :=
    35	  MvPolynomial.degreeOf_le_iff.mpr fun s hs =>
    36	    (MvPolynomial.mem_restrictDegree (σ := Fin m) (R := K) p d).mp hp s hs i
    37	
    38	/-- Paper label `rem:individual-degree-convention`.
    39	
    40	Increasing the individual-degree bound enlarges the corresponding low-degree
    41	polynomial class. -/
    42	theorem polyFuncMonotone {m d : ℕ} {K : Type*} [CommSemiring K] :
    43	    polyFunc m K d ≤ polyFunc m K (d + 1) := by
    44	  intro p hp
    45	  rw [MvPolynomial.mem_restrictDegree] at hp ⊢
    46	  intro s hs i
    47	  exact (hp s hs i).trans (Nat.le_succ d)
    48	
    49	/-- The uniform agreement probability of two polynomials on `K^m`, written as a
    50	finite cardinality ratio over `K^m`. -/
    51	noncomputable def polynomialAgreementProbability (m : ℕ) (K : Type*) [Field K] [Fintype K]
    52	    [DecidableEq K] (g h : MvPolynomial (Fin m) K) : ℚ≥0 :=
    53	  #{x ∈ (Finset.univ : Finset (Fin m → K)) |
    54	      MvPolynomial.eval x g = MvPolynomial.eval x h} /
    55	    (Fintype.card K ^ m : ℚ≥0)
    56	
    57	/-- If every individual degree of `p` is at most `d`, then the total degree of
    58	`p` is at most `m * d`. -/
    59	theorem totalDegree_le_mul_of_degreeOf_le {m d : ℕ} {K : Type*} [CommSemiring K]
    60	    {p : MvPolynomial (Fin m) K} (hdeg : ∀ i, p.degreeOf i ≤ d) :
    61	    p.totalDegree ≤ m * d := by
    62	  rw [MvPolynomial.totalDegree]
    63	  refine Finset.sup_le ?_
    64	  intro s hs
    65	  calc
    66	    s.sum (fun _ e => e) = ∑ i : Fin m, s i := by
    67	      rw [Finsupp.sum_fintype]
    68	      intro i
    69	      rfl
    70	    _ ≤ ∑ _i : Fin m, d := by
    71	      refine Finset.sum_le_sum ?_
    72	      intro i _
    73	      exact (MvPolynomial.degreeOf_le_iff.mp (hdeg i)) s hs
    74	    _ = m * d := by
    75	      simp [Fintype.card_fin]
    76	
    77	/-- If two polynomials on `K^m` have total degree at most `d`, then the uniform
    78	agreement probability is at most `d / |K|`. -/
    79	theorem schwartzZippel_totalDegree {m d : ℕ} {K : Type*} [Field K] [Fintype K]
    80	    [DecidableEq K] {g h : MvPolynomial (Fin m) K} (hneq : g ≠ h)
    81	    (hg : g.totalDegree ≤ d) (hh : h.totalDegree ≤ d) :
    82	    polynomialAgreementProbability m K g h ≤ d / Fintype.card K := by
    83	  have hsub_ne : g - h ≠ 0 := sub_ne_zero.mpr hneq
    84	  have hsub_deg : (g - h).totalDegree ≤ d :=
    85	    (MvPolynomial.totalDegree_sub g h).trans (max_le hg hh)
    86	  unfold polynomialAgreementProbability
    87	  rw [show {x ∈ (Finset.univ : Finset (Fin m → K)) |
    88	        MvPolynomial.eval x g = MvPolynomial.eval x h} =
    89	      {x ∈ (Finset.univ : Finset (Fin m → K)) |
    90	        MvPolynomial.eval x (g - h) = 0} by
    91	        ext x
    92	        simp [MvPolynomial.eval_sub, sub_eq_zero]]
    93	  calc
    94	    #{x ∈ (Finset.univ : Finset (Fin m → K)) |
    95	        MvPolynomial.eval x (g - h) = 0} /
    96	        (Fintype.card K ^ m : ℚ≥0)
    97	      ≤ (g - h).totalDegree / Fintype.card K := by
    98	          simpa using
    99	            (MvPolynomial.schwartz_zippel_totalDegree
   100	              (n := m) (p := g - h) hsub_ne (Finset.univ : Finset K))
   101	    _ ≤ d / Fintype.card K := by
   102	          gcongr
   103	
   104	/-- Schwartz-Zippel for the paper's low-individual-degree class
   105	`\polyfunc{m}{q}{d}`. -/
   106	theorem schwartzZippel_individualDegree {m d : ℕ} {K : Type*} [Field K] [Fintype K]
   107	    [DecidableEq K] (g h : polyFunc m K d) (hneq : g ≠ h) :
   108	    polynomialAgreementProbability m K g.1 h.1 ≤ ((m * d : ℕ) : ℚ≥0) / Fintype.card K := by
   109	  have hval_ne : g.1 ≠ h.1 := by
   110	    intro hgh
   111	    apply hneq
   112	    exact Subtype.ext hgh
   113	  have hg_degOf : ∀ i, g.1.degreeOf i ≤ d :=
   114	    degreeOf_le_of_mem_polyFunc g.property
   115	  have hh_degOf : ∀ i, h.1.degreeOf i ≤ d :=
   116	    degreeOf_le_of_mem_polyFunc h.property
   117	  exact schwartzZippel_totalDegree (g := g.1) (h := h.1) hval_ne
   118	    (totalDegree_le_mul_of_degreeOf_le hg_degOf)
   119	    (totalDegree_le_mul_of_degreeOf_le hh_degOf)
   120	
   121	end MIPStarRE.LDT.Preliminaries

1	\chapter{Strategy observables and the expanded space}
     2	\label{chap:qpbt-observables}
     3	% This chapter covers the first three subsections of the source appendix
     4	% ``Analysis of the Pauli basis test''
     5	% (references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex, lines 1-679).
     6	% The paper's subsection labels sec:qld-prelim, sec:commutation and
     7	% sec:expanding are kept on the sections below for cross-reference fidelity.
     8	% The source restates thm:pauli verbatim at the head of the appendix under the
     9	% label thm:pauli-appendix (lines 6-20); no duplicate node is created here,
    10	% and all references go to thm:pauli in Chapter chap:qpbt-test.
    11	
    12	This chapter and the two that follow contain the proof of the soundness
    13	theorem for the Pauli basis test, Theorem~\ref{thm:pauli}, stated in
    14	Chapter~\ref{chap:qpbt-test}. Starting from a strategy that succeeds in the
    15	game $G^{\mathrm{Pauli}}_{(q,m,d)}$ with high probability, the proof
    16	constructs a representation of the Pauli group on the players' Hilbert space
    17	in several stages. In Section~\ref{sec:commutation} the strategy measurements
    18	are used to define a set of observables that correspond to a subset of the
    19	Pauli $X$ and $Z$ observables, and these observables are shown to
    20	approximately satisfy the associated Pauli group relations. In
    21	Section~\ref{sec:expanding}, ancillary registers containing EPR states are
    22	adjoined to the players' state, and a new set of approximately commuting
    23	observables acting on the expanded state is defined.
    24	Chapter~\ref{chap:qpbt-combining} combines the approximately commuting
    25	observables into a strategy for the \emph{classical} low individual degree
    26	test and applies the soundness theorem of that test to construct a single
    27	projective measurement that simultaneously measures all of them.
    28	Chapter~\ref{chap:qpbt-extraction} uses this simultaneous measurement to
    29	construct an exact representation of the Pauli group, shows that it is close
    30	to the original strategy observables on the expanded state, and deduces
    31	Theorem~\ref{thm:pauli}. Section~\ref{sec:qld-prelim} below collects
    32	preliminary definitions and lemmas used throughout the analysis.
    33	
    34	\section{Preliminaries}
    35	\label{sec:qld-prelim}
    36	
    37	\begin{definition}[Individual and total degree polynomial classes]
    38		\label{def:ideg-deg-polynomials}
    39		\uses{def:line, def:line-representative, def:polyfunc}
    40		Given integers $d, m \geq 0$ and a prime power $q$, denote by
    41		$\mathrm{ideg}_{d,m}(\F_q)$ the set of polynomials in $m$ variables over
    42		$\F_q$ with \emph{individual} degree at most $d$ in each variable. When
    43		the field is clear from context we write $\mathrm{ideg}_{d,m}$, and when
    44		the number of variables is also clear from context, $\mathrm{ideg}_d$. We
    45		denote by $\deg_d$ the set of polynomials with \emph{total} degree at
    46		most $d$.
    47		% The line-restricted classes below are introduced only implicitly in the
    48		% source, in the statement of the lemma labelled lem:qld-comm-line-cons,
    49		% which reads them as polynomials "defined on the line". The coefficient
    50		% reading adopted here follows the answer format of the decision procedure
    51		% of the low individual degree game (source figure fig:ld-decider) and the
    52		% representative convention of def:polyfunc; see the remark following this
    53		% definition.
    54		For a line $\ell \subseteq \F_q^m$ (Definition~\ref{def:line}) presented
    55		by a base point $u_0$ and a direction $v$ --- for the lines arising as
    56		question contents, the pair read off the line's description, whose base
    57		point is the canonical representative of
    58		Definition~\ref{def:line-representative} --- and an integer $c \geq 0$,
    59		we write $\deg_c(\ell)$ for the set of univariate polynomials of degree
    60		at most $c$, each given by its list of $c+1$ coefficients and identified
    61		by its polynomial representative rather than by the function it induces,
    62		as in Definition~\ref{def:polyfunc}; the argument $\ell$ records the
    63		line to which such an answer refers, through the parameterization
    64		$t \mapsto u_0 + tv$. The cases used below are $\deg_d(\ell)$ and
    65		$\deg_{md}(\ell)$; whenever $d \leq md$, extending coefficient lists by
    66		zeros gives the inclusion $\deg_d(\ell) \subseteq \deg_{md}(\ell)$. For
    67		$f \in \deg_c(\ell)$, $u \in \ell$, and $a \in \F_q$, we say that $f$
    68		\emph{evaluates to $a$ at $u$}, written $f(u) = a$, if $f(t) = a$ for
    69		every $t \in \F_q$ with $u = u_0 + tv$. When $v \neq 0$ this $t$ is
    70		unique, so every $f$ evaluates at every point of $\ell$; when $v = 0$,
    71		so that $\ell = \{u_0\}$, exactly those $f$ that induce a constant
    72		function on $\F_q$ evaluate at $u_0$, to their constant value. An
    73		operator indexed by $f(u)$ is understood to be the zero operator when
    74		$f$ does not evaluate at $u$, and for a family $\{N_f\}$ indexed by
    75		$f \in \deg_c(\ell)$ we write
    76		$N_{[\mathrm{eval}_u(\cdot)=a]} = \sum_{f \colon f(u) = a} N_f$; when
    77		$v = 0$ the classes indexed by $a \in \F_q$ form a sub-measurement
    78		rather than a partition of the outcomes.
    79	\end{definition}
    80	
    81	\begin{remark}[Line answers as coefficient lists]
    82		\label{rem:deg-line-representatives}
    83		The source refers to the elements of $\deg_{md}(\ell)$ as polynomials
    84		``defined on the line $\ell$'', that is, as functions on the point set
    85		of $\ell$, while its decision procedure expects each line answer as a
    86		list of coefficients. The two readings differ. When $md \geq q$,
    87		distinct coefficient lists induce the same function $\F_q \to \F_q$;
    88		and when $\ell$ has direction $v = 0$ --- a case the question
    89		distributions produce with positive probability
    90		(Remark~\ref{rem:ld-win-zero-direction}) --- the point set of $\ell$ is
    91		the singleton $\{u_0\}$, so a function on $\ell$ retains only a single
    92		field element of the answer. Definition~\ref{def:ideg-deg-polynomials}
    93		therefore adopts the coefficient reading, under which the strategy's
    94		line measurements are indexed by exactly the answers of the prescribed
    95		form, and its evaluation convention reproduces the universal
    96		quantification of the line-versus-point clauses of the win predicates
    97		(Definition~\ref{def:ld-win-predicate}).
    98	\end{remark}

   100	Throughout this chapter $q = 2^k$ with $k$ odd is an admissible field size
   101	(Definition~\ref{def:admissible-size}) and $n = 2^m$. Recall from
   102	Chapter~\ref{chap:qpbt-algebra} the low-degree code
   103	(see Definition~\ref{def:low-degree-encoding}), which maps each vector
   104	$h \in \F_q^{n}$, with
   105	coordinates indexed by binary strings of length $m$, to a polynomial
   106	$g_h \in \mathrm{ideg}_{d,m}(\F_q)$ such that $g_h(u) = h_u$ for every
   107	$u \in \{0,1\}^m$; for $x \in \F_q^m$ the associated vector
   108	$\mathrm{ind}_m(x) \in \F_q^{n}$ satisfies
   109	$g_h(x) = h \cdot \mathrm{ind}_m(x)$ for all $h$. Recall also the finite
   110	field trace $\tr = \tr_{q \to 2} \colon \F_q \to \F_2$
   111	(see Definition~\ref{def:subfield-trace}).
   112	
   113	\begin{definition}[Commuting and anticommuting tuples]
   114		\label{def:anticommuting-tuple}
   115		% The quantity gamma is introduced in the source at eq:gamma-value, inside
   116		% the completeness analysis of the Pauli basis test; that label has no
   117		% corresponding node here, so the definition below is self-contained.
   118		\uses{def:low-degree-encoding, def:subfield-trace}
   119		For a tuple
   120		$\omega = (u_X, u_Z, r_X, r_Z) \in (\F_q^m)^2 \times (\F_q)^2$, let
   121		\[
   122			\gamma(\omega) \,=\, \tr\big( (r_X \cdot \mathrm{ind}_m(u_X)) \cdot (r_Z \cdot \mathrm{ind}_m(u_Z)) \big)\,,
   123		\]
   124		where $r_W \cdot \mathrm{ind}_m(u_W)$ is the scalar multiple of the
   125		vector $\mathrm{ind}_m(u_W) \in \F_q^{n}$, the middle $\cdot$ is the
   126		$\F_q$-inner product of two vectors in $\F_q^{n}$, and
   127		$\tr = \tr_{q \to 2}$. The tuple $\omega$ is called \emph{anticommuting}
   128		if $\gamma(\omega) \neq 0$, and \emph{commuting} if $\gamma(\omega) = 0$.
   129	\end{definition}
   130	
   131	The sign $(-1)^{\gamma(\omega)}$ is exactly the sign with which the
   132	generalized Pauli observables $\tau^X(r_X \cdot \mathrm{ind}_m(u_X))$ and
   133	$\tau^Z(r_Z \cdot \mathrm{ind}_m(u_Z))$ commute
   134	(see Lemma~\ref{lem:twisted-commutation});
   135	this is the source of the terminology.
   136

   541	\begin{lemma}[The sub-line distribution]
   542		\label{lem:qld-sublines}
   543		\uses{def:line, def:line-point-dist, def:ith-restricted-line}
   544		% Statement as in the source (references/qpbt-paper/
   545		% 14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex, lem:qld-sublines). The
   546		% line-point distribution over F_q^{2m+2} is built from the index
   547		% function chi of def:ld-question-distribution at dimension 2m+2, which
   548		% is defined only when 2m+2 divides q; the source instantiates it
   549		% without securing this condition. See rem:qld-4-7-divisibility.
   550		There exists a distribution $D$
   551		over tuples $(\ell, \ell_X, \ell_Z)$, where $\ell$ is a line in
   552		$\F_q^{2m+2}$ and $\ell_X, \ell_Z$ are lines in $\F_q^m$, with the
   553		following properties:
   554		\begin{enumerate}
   555			\item The marginal distribution over $\ell$ is the same as the
   556			marginal of the line-point distribution over $\F_q^{2m+2}$.
   557			% The source phrases the next property as: the marginal over
   558			% (ell_X, ell_Z) is "a mixture of the product distributions
   559			% D_{ALine,i} x D_{ALine,j} and D_{DLine,i} x D_{DLine,j}". Those
   560			% products are distributions over pairs of line-point pairs, not
   561			% over pairs of lines, so the phrase does not define the asserted
   562			% marginal distribution on pairs of lines as written; the
   563			% formulation below states the mixture at the level of the joint
   564			% law of (ell_X, ell_Z, u), which is what the proofs of
   565			% lem:claim-17-2 and lem:claim-17-3 use.
   566			\item For any point of the form $u = (u_X, u_Z, \alpha, \beta)$
   567			lying on $\ell$, it holds that $u_X \in \ell_X$ and
   568			$u_Z \in \ell_Z$. Moreover, the joint distribution of
   569			$(\ell_X, \ell_Z, u)$, for $(\ell, \ell_X, \ell_Z) \sim D$ and
   570			$u$ chosen uniformly at random on $\ell$, is a mixture of
   571			components indexed by a type
   572			$\mathrm{v} \in \{\mathrm{ALine}, \mathrm{DLine}\}$ and indices
   573			$i, j \in \{1, \dots, m\}$ with the following two properties
   574			within the component $(\mathrm{v}, i, j)$: the pair
   575			$(\ell_X, \ell_Z)$ is distributed according to the product of the
   576			marginal distributions on lines of $D_{\mathrm{v},i}$ and of
   577			$D_{\mathrm{v},j}$, and, conditioned on $(\ell_X, \ell_Z)$, the
   578			point $u_X$ is uniformly distributed on $\ell_X$ and likewise the
   579			point $u_Z$ is uniformly distributed on $\ell_Z$. Equivalently,
   580			since under each restricted distribution the point is uniformly
   581			distributed on the line conditionally on the line: within the
   582			component $(\mathrm{v}, i, j)$, the pair
   583			$((\ell_X, u_X), (\ell_Z, z'))$, where $z'$ is a uniformly random
   584			point of $\ell_Z$ sampled independently of $u$, is distributed
   585			according to $D_{\mathrm{v},i} \times D_{\mathrm{v},j}$, and
   586			symmetrically the pair $((\ell_X, x'), (\ell_Z, u_Z))$, with $x'$
   587			a uniformly random point of $\ell_X$ sampled independently of
   588			$u$, is distributed according to
   589			$D_{\mathrm{v},i} \times D_{\mathrm{v},j}$. (No assertion is made
   590			about the joint conditional law of the pair $(u_X, u_Z)$.)
   591			\item If $\ell$ is axis-parallel, then $\ell_X$ and $\ell_Z$ are
   592			axis-parallel.
   593		\end{enumerate}
   594		(Property~3 is not part of the numbered statement in the source; see
   595		Remark~\ref{rem:qld-sublines-property-three}.)
   596	\end{lemma}

   598		\uses{def:line-representative, def:ld-question-distribution,

   256	The Pauli basis test is the quantum low individual degree test of Natarajan and Vidick, in the slightly modified form introduced by Natarajan and Wright~\cite{Natarajan2018NEEXP}. Informally, the test certifies that the players share the state $\ket{\mathrm{EPR}_q}^{\ot M}$, where $M = 2^m$. On a question of type $(\mathsf{Pauli}, W)$ with $W \in \{X,Z\}$, a player is expected to measure the generalized Pauli basis POVM $\{\tau^W_h\}_{h \in \F_q^M}$ of Chapter~\ref{chap:qpbt-algebra} and report the outcome $h$. Most subtests probe limited information about $h$: given a point $u_W \in \F_q^m$, a player is expected to report the evaluation $g_h(u_W)$ of the low-degree encoding $g_h$ of $h$, and for a fixed basis $W$ these probes are checked against each other by the classical low individual degree game of Section~\ref{sec:ld-verifier}. Consistency \emph{between} the two bases is checked through two-outcome probes: given additionally $r_W \in \F_q$, a player reports $\tr(g_h(u_W)\, r_W) \in \F_2$. The two binary measurements obtained in this way for $W = X$ and $W = Z$ either commute or anticommute, according to the value $\gamma \in \F_2$ of Equation~\eqref{eq:gamma-value} below. When $\gamma = 0$ the verifier checks commutation directly by asking for both bits simultaneously; when $\gamma = 1$ the verifier checks anticommutation by playing the Magic Square game, using Theorem~\ref{thm:ms-from-ac}.

1:\chapter{Strategy observables and the expanded space}
3:% This chapter covers the first three subsections of the source appendix
4:% ``Analysis of the Pauli basis test''
5:% (references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex, lines 1-679).
6:% The paper's subsection labels sec:qld-prelim, sec:commutation and
7:% sec:expanding are kept on the sections below for cross-reference fidelity.
8:% The source restates thm:pauli verbatim at the head of the appendix under the
9:% label thm:pauli-appendix (lines 6-20); no duplicate node is created here,
10:% and all references go to thm:pauli in Chapter chap:qpbt-test.
12:This chapter and the two that follow contain the proof of the soundness
13:theorem for the Pauli basis test, Theorem~\ref{thm:pauli}, stated in
14:Chapter~\ref{chap:qpbt-test}. Starting from a strategy that succeeds in the
16:constructs a representation of the Pauli group on the players' Hilbert space
17:in several stages. In Section~\ref{sec:commutation} the strategy measurements
18:are used to define a set of observables that correspond to a subset of the
19:Pauli $X$ and $Z$ observables, and these observables are shown to
20:approximately satisfy the associated Pauli group relations. In
21:Section~\ref{sec:expanding}, ancillary registers containing EPR states are
22:adjoined to the players' state, and a new set of approximately commuting
23:observables acting on the expanded state is defined.
24:Chapter~\ref{chap:qpbt-combining} combines the approximately commuting
25:observables into a strategy for the \emph{classical} low individual degree
26:test and applies the soundness theorem of that test to construct a single
27:projective measurement that simultaneously measures all of them.
28:Chapter~\ref{chap:qpbt-extraction} uses this simultaneous measurement to
29:construct an exact representation of the Pauli group, shows that it is close
30:to the original strategy observables on the expanded state, and deduces
31:Theorem~\ref{thm:pauli}. Section~\ref{sec:qld-prelim} below collects
32:preliminary definitions and lemmas used throughout the analysis.
34:\section{Preliminaries}
37:\begin{definition}[Individual and total degree polynomial classes]
38:	\label{def:ideg-deg-polynomials}
39:	\uses{def:line, def:line-representative, def:polyfunc}
40:	Given integers $d, m \geq 0$ and a prime power $q$, denote by
41:	$\mathrm{ideg}_{d,m}(\F_q)$ the set of polynomials in $m$ variables over
42:	$\F_q$ with \emph{individual} degree at most $d$ in each variable. When
43:	the field is clear from context we write $\mathrm{ideg}_{d,m}$, and when
44:	the number of variables is also clear from context, $\mathrm{ideg}_d$. We
45:	denote by $\deg_d$ the set of polynomials with \emph{total} degree at
47:	% The line-restricted classes below are introduced only implicitly in the
48:	% source, in the statement of the lemma labelled lem:qld-comm-line-cons,
49:	% which reads them as polynomials "defined on the line". The coefficient
50:	% reading adopted here follows the answer format of the decision procedure
51:	% of the low individual degree game (source figure fig:ld-decider) and the
52:	% representative convention of def:polyfunc; see the remark following this
53:	% definition.
54:	For a line $\ell \subseteq \F_q^m$ (Definition~\ref{def:line}) presented
55:	by a base point $u_0$ and a direction $v$ --- for the lines arising as
56:	question contents, the pair read off the line's description, whose base
57:	point is the canonical representative of
58:	Definition~\ref{def:line-representative} --- and an integer $c \geq 0$,
59:	we write $\deg_c(\ell)$ for the set of univariate polynomials of degree
60:	at most $c$, each given by its list of $c+1$ coefficients and identified
61:	by its polynomial representative rather than by the function it induces,
62:	as in Definition~\ref{def:polyfunc}; the argument $\ell$ records the
63:	line to which such an answer refers, through the parameterization
64:	$t \mapsto u_0 + tv$. The cases used below are $\deg_d(\ell)$ and
65:	$\deg_{md}(\ell)$; whenever $d \leq md$, extending coefficient lists by
66:	zeros gives the inclusion $\deg_d(\ell) \subseteq \deg_{md}(\ell)$. For
67:	$f \in \deg_c(\ell)$, $u \in \ell$, and $a \in \F_q$, we say that $f$
68:	\emph{evaluates to $a$ at $u$}, written $f(u) = a$, if $f(t) = a$ for
69:	every $t \in \F_q$ with $u = u_0 + tv$. When $v \neq 0$ this $t$ is
70:	unique, so every $f$ evaluates at every point of $\ell$; when $v = 0$,
71:	so that $\ell = \{u_0\}$, exactly those $f$ that induce a constant
72:	function on $\F_q$ evaluate at $u_0$, to their constant value. An
73:	operator indexed by $f(u)$ is understood to be the zero operator when
74:	$f$ does not evaluate at $u$, and for a family $\{N_f\}$ indexed by
75:	$f \in \deg_c(\ell)$ we write
76:	$N_{[\mathrm{eval}_u(\cdot)=a]} = \sum_{f \colon f(u) = a} N_f$; when
77:	$v = 0$ the classes indexed by $a \in \F_q$ form a sub-measurement
78:	rather than a partition of the outcomes.
79:\end{definition}
81:\begin{remark}[Line answers as coefficient lists]
82:	\label{rem:deg-line-representatives}
83:	The source refers to the elements of $\deg_{md}(\ell)$ as polynomials
84:	``defined on the line $\ell$'', that is, as functions on the point set
85:	of $\ell$, while its decision procedure expects each line answer as a
86:	list of coefficients. The two readings differ. When $md \geq q$,
87:	distinct coefficient lists induce the same function $\F_q \to \F_q$;
88:	and when $\ell$ has direction $v = 0$ --- a case the question
89:	distributions produce with positive probability
90:	(Remark~\ref{rem:ld-win-zero-direction}) --- the point set of $\ell$ is
91:	the singleton $\{u_0\}$, so a function on $\ell$ retains only a single
92:	field element of the answer. Definition~\ref{def:ideg-deg-polynomials}
93:	therefore adopts the coefficient reading, under which the strategy's
94:	line measurements are indexed by exactly the answers of the prescribed
95:	form, and its evaluation convention reproduces the universal
96:	quantification of the line-versus-point clauses of the win predicates
97:	(Definition~\ref{def:ld-win-predicate}).
98:\end{remark}
100:Throughout this chapter $q = 2^k$ with $k$ odd is an admissible field size
101:(Definition~\ref{def:admissible-size}) and $n = 2^m$. Recall from
103:(see Definition~\ref{def:low-degree-encoding}), which maps each vector
104:$h \in \F_q^{n}$, with
105:coordinates indexed by binary strings of length $m$, to a polynomial
106:$g_h \in \mathrm{ideg}_{d,m}(\F_q)$ such that $g_h(u) = h_u$ for every
107:$u \in \{0,1\}^m$; for $x \in \F_q^m$ the associated vector
108:$\mathrm{ind}_m(x) \in \F_q^{n}$ satisfies

- [ ] F1 (changes) `blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:27` — Game notation drifts from the source’s `\mathfrak G` and changes again across Chapters 14 and 16.
- [ ] F2 (changes) `blueprint/src/chapter/ch14_qpbt_observables.tex:101` — The symbol `n = 2^m` silently renames the source and surrounding chapters’ quantity `M = 2^m`.

- [ ] F4 (changes) `blueprint/src/chapter/ch16_qpbt_extraction.tex:28` — Pointwise decoder–encoder equality does not characterize encodings when `d ≥ q`.

## Review

F4 is the substantive mathematical issue. For the admissible tuple \((q,m,d)=(8,1,8)\), take \(g(x)=x^8\). This polynomial representative is not multilinear and hence is not an encoding, but \(\mathrm{Dec}(g)=(0,1)\), so
\[
\mathrm{Dec}(g)\cdot\mathrm{ind}_1(u)=u=u^8=g(u)
\]
for every \(u\in\mathbb F_8\). Thus the claim that the identity “holds exactly when \(g\) is an encoding, and fails otherwise” is false. Line 20’s assertion that the two sides are distinct as functions is false for the same reason. State instead that \(g_{\mathrm{Dec}(g)}=g\) as polynomial representatives exactly for encodings, while their induced functions may agree for nonencodings when \(d\ge q\).

For F1, the source defines `\game` as `\mathfrak{G}` and consistently uses it for the low-degree, Magic Square, and Pauli games. Chapter 13 uses `\mathcal G`, Chapter 14 uses bare `G`, and Chapter 16 returns to `\mathfrak G`; bare \(G\) also conflicts with the notation for type graphs. Standardize the games as \(\mathfrak G^{\mathrm{ld}}\), \(\mathfrak G^{\mathrm{MS}}\), and \(\mathfrak G^{\mathrm{Pauli}}\), reserving \(G\) for graphs.

For F2, the source’s `\nqubits` expands to \(M\), and Chapters 13 and 16 likewise use \(M=2^m\). Either use \(M\) throughout Chapter 14 or explicitly introduce \(n=M=2^m\) and identify \(M\) as the source notation.

For F3, the corresponding source passage is ordinary setup prose. The block introduces no mathematical object: it fixes parameters and a strategy, then applies the already cited Naimark theorem. Replace the definition environment with an unnumbered standing-setup paragraph and update references that currently call it a definition.

The sole changed-chapter `\lean`/`\leanok` link, `MIPStarRE.Quantum.Measurement.postprocess`, is accurate: arbitrary outcome relabeling, fiber summation, and completeness agree with the blueprint statement. Its finiteness and decidable-equality assumptions are faithful boundary conditions. There are no stale `\notready` tags or newly changed Lean declarations requiring status updates. The Schwartz–Zippel restatement correctly remains unlinked because its reduced polynomial-function formulation does not match the existing theorem’s public `MvPolynomial` signature.

No new banned-language or Lean-jargon findings were found. Previously raised feedback was not duplicated. Count: 4 category-A findings, 0 status-tag errors, 0 new category-B findings.
